At half past six on Friday, the Kolkata ad agency was emptying. Jyoti waved from the lift. “Weekend, finally!” Two others followed her, laughing.
Mr Ghosh stopped at Seema's desk with a folder. “The tea brand pitch moved to Monday. I need someone who won't let me down.” He smiled. “That's always you, Seema.”
Seema's weekend plans, her cousin's engagement, flashed in her mind. She took the folder anyway.
Alone under the office lights, she felt her jaw tighten. Why is it never Jyoti? she thought. And yet, some small part of her glowed. He trusts me. Nobody else could do this.
She worked till eleven, annoyed and oddly proud at the same time.

qa.a: It was half past six on Friday.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Seema have working alone?
qa.a: She felt used and resentful that it was never Jyoti, but also oddly proud that her boss trusted only her.

qa.q: What could Seema say next time she's handed extra work?
qa.a: She could say calmly that she has plans and ask whether the work can be shared with Jyoti or another colleague.

qa.q: How might Mr Ghosh see his habit of giving Seema extra work?
qa.a: He probably sees it as a compliment and an easy fix, not noticing it overloads her while others coast.

grounding: Shows a dependable worker given extra work because she always delivers, feeling used but also proud of being needed.

I'm Pooja, and by my third year at the school I had become the teacher who said yes.
Annual day? Pooja will do it. Exam papers for three sections? Pooja. When a colleague went on leave, Aparna ma'am, our principal, gave me her classes too. “You never disappoint me,” she said. Others in the staffroom drank their tea and talked about weekend trips.
I remember walking home one evening with a bag of fifty answer sheets, furious. Why me? Why always me?
And yet, I also remember the warmth when Aparna ma'am thanked me at assembly. Being needed felt good. That was the trap.
It took me a whole year to say, “Ma'am, I can't take this one.” She was surprised, and then she gave it to someone else.

qa.a: Pooja was carrying fifty answer sheets.

So you asked what surprised me about managing? I'm Siddharth, and it was noticing who carried whom.
On my first project as a manager, Maria stayed late every night. Rohit left at five sharp and his updates were always “in progress”. When I checked the files, Maria had done nearly all the design, and even fixed Rohit's parts.

The four new flatmates in the Indiranagar flat sat on the floor with pizza on their first Sunday. Avni pulled out a notebook.

Arnab groaned. “We're adults. It'll work out.”
